key_terms.meaning: The part of heat Q drawn from a source at T that can be converted to work with surroundings at T₀: Q(1 − T₀/T), in kJ.
The part T₀ΔS of the heat Q that must be dumped to the surroundings and can never become work, in kJ.
The condition where a system sits at the pressure p₀ and temperature T₀ of its surroundings, so no further work can be drawn from it.
A body so large that giving or taking heat does not change its temperature.
The maximum useful work a system or a stream can deliver as it comes to the dead state, usually written Φ = (U − U₀) + p₀(V − V₀) − T₀(S − S₀).
Exergy carried by a stream, ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) + V²/2 + gz, in kJ/kg.
Useful work lost to friction, mixing or finite-temperature heat transfer: I = T₀ S_gen, in kJ.
Ratio of the least exergy input needed to the exergy actually supplied, η_II = η/η_rev, always ≤ 1.
A = U − TS, a property in kJ; its fall at constant T and V equals the maximum work obtainable.
G = H − TS, a property in kJ; its fall at constant T and p equals the maximum non-expansion work obtainable.
A process that goes on its own; at constant T,V it needs ΔA < 0 and at constant T,p it needs ΔG < 0.
μ_i = (∂G/∂n_i) at fixed T, p and other amounts; the per-mole escape tendency of species i that drives phase and reaction equilibrium.
A differential dF = M dx + N dy for which ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x, so the value of F depends only on the end states.
Four equalities among second derivatives of U, H, A, G, for example (∂T/∂V)_S = −(∂p/∂S)_V, linking entropy to p, v, T data.
T dS = dU + p dV and T dS = dH − V dp, in kJ; the starting point for all the Maxwell relations.
μ_JT = (∂T/∂p)_h, in K/Pa; zero for an ideal gas, and positive below a gas's inversion temperature.
dp/dT = h_fg/(T v_fg), the slope of a saturation line on a p–T diagram.
Enthalpy change per kg when a saturated liquid turns to saturated vapour at constant T and p, in kJ/kg.
The single temperature and pressure where solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium — 273.16 K and 611.7 Pa for water.

takeaways: Of any heat Q from a source at T, only Q(1 − T₀/T) is available as work; the rest, T₀ΔS, is thrown to the surroundings.
Available energy grows with source temperature, so the same 100 kJ of heat is worth more at 800 K than at 400 K.
Exergy is measured from the dead state; it is destroyed by irreversibility at the rate T₀ S_gen, and it is never created.
Second-law efficiency tells you how close a device is to the best possible device, while first-law efficiency only compares output to input.
At constant T and V the Helmholtz function must fall for a process to be spontaneous; at constant T and p the Gibbs function must fall.
Maxwell relations turn entropy, which is hard to measure, into pressure, volume and temperature slopes, which are easy to measure.
TdS equations plus Maxwell relations give entropy changes of real gases and liquids from p–v–T data alone.
At phase equilibrium the Gibbs functions of the two phases are equal, and differentiating that equality gives the Clausius–Clapeyron equation.
bank_note: Long answers here are derivation-led: examiners want the availability formula with its two parts labelled, the four potentials defined and used as criteria, the Maxwell relations derived from exact differentials, and Clausius–Clapeyron obtained from equality of Gibbs functions, each followed by one worked use.

bank.q: Heat Q is taken from a source at temperature T while the surroundings sit at T₀. Show that the maximum work obtainable is Q(1 − T₀/T) and identify the unavailable part.
outline: Put a reversible engine between source and surroundings; efficiency is 1 − T₀/T
Available energy W_max = Q(1 − T₀/T)
Unavailable energy = Q − W_max = Q T₀/T = T₀ΔS, where ΔS = Q/T is the entropy drop of the source
State that unavailable energy is the heat rejected to the surroundings
Note that availability rises as T rises and falls to zero as T → T₀

bank.q: Define the Helmholtz and Gibbs functions. Use each to state the criterion for spontaneous change at constant temperature with constant volume, and with constant pressure.
outline: A = U − TS and G = H − TS, both properties in kJ
At constant T, ΔA = ΔU − TΔS; first law gives ΔU = Q − W, so −ΔA is the maximum work
Spontaneous at constant T,V when ΔA < 0; equilibrium when ΔA = 0
At constant T,p, −ΔG is maximum non-expansion work (shaft work)
Spontaneous at constant T,p when ΔG < 0; equilibrium when ΔG = 0
Mention that G is the more useful potential for chemical and phase change

bank.q: What are Maxwell relations? Derive any two of them from the exactness of the thermodynamic differentials.
outline: Write dU = T dS − p dV, dH = T dS + V dp, dA = −S dT − p dV, dG = −S dT + V dp
For an exact differential dF = M dx + N dy, ∂M/∂y = ∂N/∂x
Apply to dA: (∂S/∂V)_T = (∂p/∂T)_V
Apply to dG: (∂S/∂p)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_p
Apply to dU and dH to get the other two relations
State the use: entropy changes from measurable p–v–T slopes

bank.q: Explain exergy and the dead state, and distinguish first-law efficiency from second-law efficiency.
outline: Exergy is the maximum useful work as the system reaches T₀, p₀
Dead state definitions; exergy is zero there
Exergy of a closed system and of a flow stream (ψ)
Exergy destroyed = T₀ S_gen (Gouy–Stodola)
First-law efficiency compares output with input; second-law compares with the reversible best
η_II = η/η_rev ≤ 1; example such as an electric heater where η_II is low but η is near 1

bank.q: Derive the Clausius–Clapeyron equation from the equality of Gibbs functions of two phases in equilibrium.
outline: At equilibrium g_f = g_g along the saturation line
Move to a neighbouring point on the line: dg_f = dg_g
Use dg = −s dT + v dp for each phase
−s_f dT + v_f dp = −s_g dT + v_g dp
(s_g − s_f) dT = (v_g − v_f) dp
Use s_fg = h_fg/T to get dp/dT = h_fg/(T v_fg)

bank.q: A reservoir at 800 K supplies 1000 kJ of heat. The surroundings are at 300 K. Find the available energy, the unavailable energy and the entropy generated if the heat is used irreversibly.
outline: Available energy = Q(1 − T₀/T) = 1000(1 − 300/800) = 625 kJ
Unavailable energy = 1000 − 625 = 375 kJ
Check with T₀ΔS, where ΔS = Q/T = 1.25 kJ/K
375 = 300 × 1.25, so the numbers agree
Any real engine delivering less than 625 kJ adds S_gen; state I = T₀ S_gen

bank.q: Steam enters a turbine at 3 MPa, 400 °C and leaves at 0.1 MPa with quality 0.95. Taking T₀ = 298 K, compute the specific flow exergy at inlet and outlet and the second-law efficiency.
outline: Look up h and s at inlet from steam tables
Find h and s at outlet using h_f + x h_fg and s_f + x s_fg
ψ = (h − h₀) − T₀(s − s₀) with h₀, s₀ of saturated liquid at 298 K
Actual work = h_in − h_out
Reversible work between the same states = ψ_in − ψ_out
η_II = actual work / reversible work

bank.q: Using a Maxwell relation, show how the entropy change of a real gas can be found from pressure–volume–temperature data, and derive the Joule–Thomson coefficient in terms of measurable quantities.
outline: Start from T dS = T(∂S/∂p)_T dp + T(∂S/∂T)_p dT
Use (∂S/∂p)_T = −(∂V/∂T)_p from the Maxwell relations
Replace the second term using c_p = T(∂S/∂T)_p
Integrate to get Δs from p, v, T and c_p data
For μ_JT use dh = c_p dT + [v − T(∂v/∂T)_p] dp at constant h
μ_JT = [T(∂v/∂T)_p − v]/c_p; it is zero for an ideal gas

bank.q: For water the saturation pressure is 101.3 kPa at 100 °C and 47.4 kPa at 80 °C. Use the Clausius–Clapeyron equation to estimate the latent heat of vaporisation near 100 °C.
outline: dp/dT ≈ Δp/ΔT from the two points, in Pa/K
Convert temperatures to kelvin
Use v_fg ≈ v_g = RT/p, neglecting v_f against v_g
h_fg = T v_fg (dp/dT)
Substitute numbers and state the answer in kJ/kg
Comment that the estimate is good away from the critical point

bank.q: Two identical rooms are warmed to the same temperature, one by a reversible heat pump and one by direct electrical heating. Compare the exergy destroyed and the second-law efficiency, and explain why the heater can still have a first-law efficiency of 1.
outline: Both deliver the same heat, so first-law efficiency looks fine for the heater
Reversible heating needs exergy input Q(1 − T₀/T_room) only
Electrical work is pure exergy, so the extra work becomes T₀ S_gen
Second-law efficiency = minimum exergy in / actual exergy in
Heater η_II = 1 − T₀/T_room, well below 1
Conclusion: first-law efficiency hides irreversibility; exergy analysis exposes it

bank.q: Derive the TdS equations and explain how, together with the Maxwell relations, they let you compute entropy changes of liquids and real gases from property data.
outline: First law for a reversible path: dQ_rev = dU + p dV and dQ_rev = T dS
Hence T dS = dU + p dV; use H = U + pV for T dS = dH − V dp
Divide by T and expand in the chosen pair of variables
Replace (∂S/∂p)_T and (∂S/∂V)_T using Maxwell relations
For a liquid use v ≈ constant and s₂ − s₁ = c ln(T₂/T₁)
For a gas use the ideal-gas forms or integrate (∂v/∂T)_p from tables

bank.q: Explain why a plant's exergy analysis points to different improvement targets than a first-law energy balance. Illustrate with a boiler, a turbine and a condenser.
outline: Energy balance conserves kJ; exergy balance destroys some
Boiler: large irreversibility from burning fuel at flame temperature against steam at lower temperature
Turbine: irreversibility from friction and throttling, given by T₀ S_gen
Condenser: heat rejected near T₀ carries little exergy but wastes a lot of energy
Exergy destruction as a percentage of fuel exergy ranks the components
Recommendation follows the ranking, not the energy losses

bank.q: From Gibbs phase equilibrium, derive the slope of the fusion line for water and explain why it is negative while the vaporisation line is positive.
outline: dp/dT = h_fg/(T v_fg) for any phase change
For melting, h_sl > 0 and v_sl < 0 because ice is less dense than water
Product gives dp/dT < 0, so pressure lowers the melting point
For vaporisation h_fg > 0 and v_fg > 0, so dp/dT > 0
Compare with the general Clausius–Clapeyron form and the triple point
Mention use in refrigeration and in skating-type pressure effects cautiously

glossary.def: Everything outside the system boundary; its temperature T₀ and pressure p₀ define the reference for exergy.
The entropy created inside a real process, always ≥ 0 and zero only for a reversible process.
The largest work a system can give between two given end states, obtained on a fully reversible path.
Work delivered to a device other than the surroundings, that is, shaft work; work spent pushing the atmosphere is excluded.
Exergy in = exergy out + exergy destroyed + change in stored exergy, for a control volume over a time interval.
Ratio of actual work of a turbine (or compressor work input) to the work of an isentropic device between the same inlet state and outlet pressure.
The combination (U + p₀V − T₀S) for a closed system, or (H − T₀S) for a stream, whose fall gives useful work.
Any property such as U, H, A or G whose decrease at fixed natural variables gives the maximum work of a process.
The pair of properties held constant for a potential: S and V for U, S and p for H, T and V for A, T and p for G.
H = U + pV, the property that accounts for both internal energy and flow work, in kJ.
β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)_p, the fractional volume change per kelvin, in 1/K.
κ = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)_T, the fractional volume drop per unit pressure rise, in 1/Pa.
Measured pressure, specific volume and temperature of a substance, from which entropy and exergy can be computed through Maxwell relations.
The state where two phases coexist without net transfer of mass, requiring equal temperature, equal pressure and equal Gibbs function per mole.
The curve on a p–T diagram along which a liquid and its vapour coexist in equilibrium.
dp/dT = s_fg/v_fg, the exact slope of any phase boundary, valid for melting and sublimation too.
Direct change from solid to vapour, described by the same Clausius–Clapeyron form with h_sg and v_sg.
The end of the saturation line, where liquid and vapour become identical so that v_fg → 0 and h_fg → 0.
Zero, because h depends on T alone; a real gas cools or warms on throttling depending on its inversion temperature.
The entropy of a perfect crystal tends to zero as the absolute temperature tends to zero, giving absolute entropy values.
Entropy measured from the zero fixed by the third law, so tables list s at 0 K as zero.
No device working in a cycle can convert all the heat from a single reservoir into work.
A fixed region in space with mass flowing in and out, used for steady-flow exergy balances.
System plus surroundings together; its entropy never decreases, and the rise equals S_gen.
